title: for, while, do-while, for-of, and for-in
hook: Loops repeat a block until a condition fails or a sequence ends. JavaScript adds for-of to walk iterable values and for-in to enumerate object keys — choosing the wrong loop is one of the most common senior-level JavaScript interview traps.

blocks.text: A **loop** runs a block repeatedly. **for** combines initialization, condition, and update — ideal when you need an index. **while** tests before each iteration; **do...while** runs at least once. **for...of** walks **iterable** values (arrays, strings, Map, Set, NodeList) yielding elements. **for...in** walks **enumerable string keys** of an object — including inherited prototype keys unless filtered. C# **foreach** maps closest to **for...of**, not for...in.

entries.plainDefinition: Iterates over values of an iterable object using the iterator protocol.
Iterates enumerable string property keys of an object — including array indices as strings.
entries.example: for (const key in obj) { ... } — not for array elements by default.

entries.plainDefinition: An object implementing Symbol.iterator so for...of and spread can consume it.
entries.example: Array, String, Map, Set, and generator functions are iterable.

entries.plainDefinition: A property flag controlling whether for...in and Object.keys include it.
entries.example: Array index properties are enumerable — for...in on arrays is usually wrong.

sections.heading: Why for-of vs for-in matters in production

blocks.text: Use **for...of** (or array methods like `.forEach`) when you want each **value** in a sequence. Use **for...in** only for plain object key enumeration — and guard with `hasOwnProperty` or `Object.hasOwn` when you must skip inherited keys. Never use **for...in** on arrays when order and numeric indices matter — it yields string keys `"0"`, `"1"` and may include prototype pollution keys. Use classic **for** when you need index math, reverse iteration, or parallel index access.

blocks.title: C# foreach maps to for...of
blocks.body: C# foreach (var row in rows) equals for (const row of rows). C# for-in has no direct equivalent — for...in is key enumeration like reflecting over property names, not foreach over List<T>.

items.title: Need index or stride?
items.body: Use for (let i = 0; ...) — skip header row, reverse, windowing.

items.title: Need each value in iterable?
items.body: Use for...of — arrays, strings, Map entries via map.entries().

items.title: Need object keys?
items.body: Use for...in with hasOwn check, or Object.keys / Object.entries.

items.title: Unknown length, condition-driven?
items.body: Use while or do...while — read stream until done.

snippet.label: for index loop and while
snippet.explanation: Classic for when index is business logic. while/do-while for open-ended conditions. Use let in for to avoid var closure bugs.

snippet.label: for...of over arrays and iterables
snippet.explanation: for...of yields values in iteration order. Map iterates entries by default. Closest to C# foreach.

snippet.label: for...in keys — object vs array trap
snippet.explanation: for...in lists enumerable keys including array indices as strings and any added properties. for...of walks values only.

snippet.label: Object.entries — modern alternative to for...in
snippet.explanation: Object.entries + for...of avoids for...in prototype issues and reads clearly in code review.

blocks.title: for-in vs for-of traps
blocks.body: Using for...in on arrays. Mutating array length heavily during for...of without understanding iterator invalidation. Using var in for (var i...) with async callbacks. Assuming for...in order is guaranteed for all keys — integer-like keys sort ascending in modern engines but spec nuances exist. Using for...in without hasOwn when prototype chain is untrusted.

blocks.title: Interview sound bite
blocks.body: for...of iterates values via iterator protocol. for...in iterates enumerable property keys. Arrays are both objects and iterables — use for...of for elements, not for...in.

interviewTakeaways: for...of: values from iterables — maps to C# foreach.
for...in: enumerable keys on objects — includes array indices as strings; avoid on arrays.
Use let in for (let i...) — per-iteration binding; var causes closure bugs.
60s: for-of = values, for-in = keys. Object.entries + for-of for plain objects. C# foreach equals for-of not for-in.
Follow-up: when would you pick a classic for loop over for...of?
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'for...in and for...of are the same' — keys vs values is the core interview distinction.
Weak: 'for...in on arrays is fine' — yields indices as strings and extra enumerable props.
Strong: 'for-of for sequences. for-in for object keys with hasOwn. Index math uses classic for. C# foreach is for-of.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: C# foreach maps to JS for...of. C# for walks indexes like JS for (int i...). No C# equivalent blindly maps to for...in.
TypeScript for...of narrows element types on arrays and typed iterables. for...in on arrays is typed as string keys — another reason to avoid it.
